11.0.s.en: 1. Job accused of pride and falsehood

11.0.0.en: 1 Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said, 2 "Should not the multitude of words be answered? and should a man full of talk be justified? 3 Should thy arrogance make men hold their peace? and when thou mockest, shall no man make thee ashamed? 4 For thou hast said, My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in thine eyes.

11.1.0.en: "Should not the multitude of words be answered? and should a man full of talk be justified?" [2]

11.1.1.en: Eliphaz began with an introduction of great dignity (Job 4:2), while Bildad was harsher in his speech to Job (Job 8:2). Zophar came and fell upon him without compassion, directing very severe words at him.

11.1.2.en: It was not possible for Zophar to accept Job's reasoning that it was God who had allowed the trials to come upon him although he was righteous (Job 9:21; 11:4; 10:7). For this contradicts all religious philosophy, both in his own time and before it. Job appeared as one who opposes all the philosophers and those who possess religious knowledge.

11.1.3.en: He began by saying, "Should not the multitude of words be answered? and should a man full of talk be justified?" Zophar thought Job to be a babbler, a man of words without deeds, not worthy to be answered, a prattler who carries no seriousness, whose speech has no thoughtfulness or balance to deserve an answer.

11.1.4.en: Bildad had already said to Job, "the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind" (Job 8:2), and in the Septuagint it reads, "The breezes of your mouth overflow in words." Here Zophar the Naamathite accuses him of babbling.

11.1.5.en: It is true that Zophar presented sound and wise opinions, but he accused Job unjustly, because he did not share his feelings as a man who was suffering greatly, and he did not examine Job's words and circumstances carefully. He accused Job of babbling and of much vain talk in order to justify himself, though what he uttered cannot be counted babbling in view of what had befallen him. And in his speech he did not justify himself, but confessed that he is a sinner (Job 9:20).

11.1.6.en: Here Zophar calls Job to be wise by sitting at the feet of the elders and listening in silence, rather than being a man of many words. St. James says, "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19). Perhaps by the elders he means his three friends. In other words, Zophar sees that he and his two companions have the right to give Job sermons, advice and counsel, and that Job has nothing to do but sit at their feet and learn from them in silence!

11.1.7.en: * Zophar did not offer a wrong opinion when he said, [A man of many words will not be able to be justified]. As long as a man lets himself speak on and on, the gravity of silence flees from him, and he loses the safe guarding of himself. For this reason it is written, "The work of righteousness shall be quietness" (Isa 32:17). So Solomon says, "A city broken down and without a wall is the man who has no rule over his spirit in speech" (Prov 25:28) [Vulgate]. He also says, "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin" (Prov 10:19). And the psalmist bears witness to this, saying, [A man of many words shall not be established in the earth] (Ps 140:11); and even the value of a true statement is lost when it is spoken without discernment...

11.1.8.en: A true statement is against the wicked if it aims at the benefit of the righteous... But the wicked cannot hear good words with patience, ignoring the correction of their life, and so they attach themselves to words in order to answer others.

11.1.9.en: * Whoever remembers the words of the blessed Job knows how groundless this accusation is... For how could he who said, "If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me" (Job 9:20) call himself clean (pure)?

11.1.11.en: Indeed the Holy Bible urged silence as far as possible if it is holy, just as it urged constructive speech. The psalmist asked for strong divine protection for his mouth, saying, "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips" (Ps 141:3).

11.1.12.en: * The Holy Spirit teaches a man to keep his whole body, from head to foot, in harmony:

11.1.13.en: so he keeps the eyes that they may look with purity...

11.1.14.en: and he keeps the tongue that it may speak only what is good, giving weight to every word, and does not allow anything defiled or sensual to mingle with his speech.

11.1.15.en: * Flee from those who bear the name of "monks and virgins" without having true understanding and good discernment. For if you mingle with them, they will not let you advance, and may even quench the warmth of your zeal, since they have no warmth but only coldness, and they walk after their own passions. If they come to you and speak with you about earthly matters according to their own passions, do not be content with this, for the Apostle Paul wrote, "Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings" (1 Thess 5:19-20), knowing that nothing quenches the Spirit more than vain talk.

11.1.16.en: St. Anthony the Great * Silence for the sake of God is good, just as speech for the sake of God is good.

11.1.17.en: Abba Poemen * When your tongue is like the tongue of Christ, and your mouth becomes the mouth of the Father, and you become a temple of the Holy Spirit, then what honor this will be! For even if your mouth were made of gold and precious stones, it would not shine as it does with the ornaments of meekness. What is more lovable than a mouth that does not know how to revile, but is accustomed to bless and to utter good words!

11.1.18.en: St. John Chrysostom * I have often spoken and regretted it, but of silence I have never once repented.

11.1.19.en: St. Arsenius the Teacher of the Sons of the Kings * The righteous man is silent, for he teaches that there is a time for silence and a time for speech (Eccl 3:7), yet he does not become dumb. Dumbness is rather a mark of the Sadducees and of everyone who teaches falsehood, for they are made dumb and do not keep silent. Though they are dumb toward the truth, they are not silent. It was thus that the Lord spoke to the sea, and not to a man, to make it dumb, rebuking it when it was stormy.

11.2.0.en: Origen "Should thy arrogance make men hold their peace? and when thou mockest (babblest), shall no man make thee ashamed?" [3]

11.2.1.en: He called him a scoffer, who mocks God by complaining against Him, and ridicules people, since he is not ashamed to deceive those around him. As he called him a mocker, Zophar thus used harsh words and described him with unseemly epithets.

11.2.2.en: Some see in Zophar's words here an indirect accusation of Eliphaz and Bildad, for it would have been fitting for them to silence him, and not leave him to babble with violent, mistaken and meaningless speech.

11.2.3.en: In his opinion, Job had behaved arrogantly with pride and vain lies, and his two friends were not able to silence him, but kept quiet instead of defending the truth.

11.2.4.en: He accuses him of "babbling," that is, "mocking" or "scoffing," by blaming God in his complaint.

11.3.0.en: "For thou hast said, My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in thine eyes" [4].

11.3.1.en: He accused Job of words he never uttered. He accused him of saying that his doctrine is pure, and he did not say this.

11.3.2.en: Job was marked by soundness of faith. It is true that at times he was carried away, longing for death because of the weight of the trial, but he never thought of suicide.

11.3.3.en: He reproached God, but he did not deny God's justice and mercies.

11.3.4.en: And he declared that he is neither wicked nor hypocritical, but he did not deny that he is a sinner awaiting forgiveness.

11.3.5.en: Job's teaching about God was far better than that of his friends.

11.3.6.en: These friends, especially Zophar, misconstrued Job's words and gave them meanings other than what was in his mind, and they did not take his circumstances into account; and had they been put in his place, they might have sinned against God.

11.4.0.en: 5 "But oh that God would speak, and open his lips with thee; 6 And that he would shew thee the secrets of wisdom! For it is double in understanding. Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth.

11.4.1.en: "But oh that God would speak, and open his lips with thee" [5].

11.4.2.en: Zophar appeals to God Himself, saying that although He is silent and has not answered Job, it is only for a time; and if He were to speak and open His lips, Job would discover that he deserves far more than what has befallen him.

11.4.3.en: How hard it is for us to set ourselves as on the divine throne, and to claim that we know what is in His mind, and to judge others, ascribing the judgment to God.

11.4.4.en: Zophar's wish was fulfilled, and God spoke with Job; He opened His lips in his defense, requiring his friends to apologize to him and to ask for his prayers on their behalf so that he would forgive them.

11.4.5.en: Truly, there is a great difference between a man opening his mouth to judge and condemn his brethren under the cover of defending the truth and bearing witness for the holy God, and God opening His mouth and speaking with man. God speaks the truth, but it is a truth full of love and practical wisdom. Frankly He rebuked Simon Peter, and even called him "Satan" when he objected to the crucifixion and death of the Lord Christ, yet He was upholding him, and He praised him when he confessed that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

11.4.6.en: The weak sinful man opens his mouth to cast his weakness and faults upon others, but God opens His mouth to give the sinner strength to confess, the possibility of repentance, and the power for continual sanctification and constant spiritual growth by the work of the Holy Spirit of God.

11.4.7.en: * The Truth says to Peter, who was still full of earthly notions, "thou savourest not the things that be of God, but the things that be of men" (Mk 8:33); and yet when he confessed well, it was said to him, "flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven" (Mt 16:17). Thus God opens His lips when He declares His will to men by an open visitation.

11.4.9.en: * Since we cannot arrogate to ourselves the office of judge because of our sins, we ought to withdraw from performing this function; for how can we, being sinners, judge and condemn others?

11.4.10.en: Therefore no one ought to judge his brother. If your soul tells you to try others, know that the Law has not appointed you a judge and prosecutor, and so by usurping this office you fall under the penalty of the Law, because you violate its sanctity...

11.4.11.en: Therefore we must take care to examine ourselves before sitting on the judgment seat to pass sentence on others, especially if we are in the position of guide and teacher.

11.4.12.en: St. Cyril the Great * God will judge in His own proper time. For the judge is insulted when a servant presumes and pronounces a sentence before knowing the decision of the judge.

11.4.13.en: * Spread your cloak over the sinner and cover him, if you cannot bear and put his burdens upon yourself.

11.4.14.en: St. Isaac the Syrian "And that he would shew thee the secrets of wisdom!"

11.5.0.en: "For it is double in understanding. Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth" [6].

11.5.1.en: Zophar sees that Job ought to have kept silent rather than accuse God of injustice for trying him while he is righteous. Zophar assured him that what had befallen him was a punishment lighter than his iniquity deserved. It was fitting therefore that he should expect more calamities.

11.5.2.en: Since Zophar felt his inability to convince Job, he desired that God would show Job the secrets of His divine wisdom and give him a double understanding, so that he might know that the chastening that had come upon him was less than it ought to be.

11.5.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) distinguishes between the knowledge of the great works of divine wisdom and the knowledge of the great hidden works of divine wisdom. It is easy for a man to enjoy knowing God's great wisdom through the nature He created for man, and His surpassing daily gifts. But the knowledge of His great hidden wisdom is hard to grasp, where God seems to have abandoned man and allows him affliction or trial. Man needs divine grace to perceive the hidden divine wisdom behind the suffering; and when man receives this knowledge it is counted a double knowledge, for he perceives God's wisdom when He gives and also when He takes away, when He grants man what he desires and also when He does not grant his request.

11.5.4.en: * [And he will declare to thee the secrets of wisdom, and that its law is double] (Job 11:6).

11.5.5.en: The works of the great wisdom are that when Almighty God governs those whom He created, He brings them to the end of the good things with which He began, and by His inspirations He helps those whom He enlightens with the light of His visitation; so it is clear to the eyes of all men that those whom He created in His utter generosity He supports with His compassions. And when He bestows spiritual gifts, He Himself leads them into perfection, those with whom He began in His "generosity" of compassions.

11.5.6.en: But the works of the great secret wisdom are when He (seems to) forsake those whom He created, when He does not complete the good works He began with us because of sin, when He enlightens us with the radiance of His shining grace, and yet allows the temptation of the flesh to strike us with a mist of blindness. When He does not care to preserve for us the good gifts He gave us, He lifts the longings of our souls toward Him, and yet presses upon us in a hidden way through the helplessness of our weak nature.

11.5.7.en: Paul was anxious to reach the secrets of this wisdom when he said, "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?" (Rom 11:33-34)... Since Paul was unable to reach the secrets of God, he returned to the knowledge of his weakness.

11.5.8.en: Zophar was learned through pursuing knowledge, but he was ignorant because of the insolence of his arrogant speech, not perceiving the truth about himself, looking upon his own weak condition as that of a virtuous person.

11.5.10.en: Zophar says that where God reveals His hidden wisdom to man, He grants him a double understanding. This is a truth enjoyed by the sincere and faithful believer. He does not cease asking God to grant him wisdom to perceive God's plan, and so he receives a double understanding.

11.5.11.en: What does he mean by double understanding?

11.5.12.en: First: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that perceiving God's hidden wisdom is not a purely theoretical, rational perception, but a knowledge of experience and life, where wisdom is bound to love. The wise man receives a double understanding, since he practices a double love, namely the love of God and the love of neighbor. He receives a double love toward God, without limit; and he receives a double love toward his brethren, so that with his whole being he longs to put his brethren before himself in everything, and desires to treat them as he wishes them to treat him.

11.5.13.en: The law of love is a double law, for we are bound to love either God or our neighbor.

11.5.14.en: As for our love for God, it ought to be a double love, for we love Him with all the heart, all the soul and all the might, so that we leave nothing for ourselves that we do not offer to God.

11.5.15.en: And as for our love for our neighbor, it is double: on the one hand we are required not to despise our neighbor through covetousness, or insult with the tongue, or contempt for the bodies of others through the selfishness of fleshly lusts; and on the other hand, to behave toward others as we would have others do to us.

11.5.16.en: * [And its law is double] (Job 11:6). By what is [the law of God] understood but love? In it we read inwardly how the commandments of life must be supported by outward works. The voice of the Truth says of this law, "This is my commandment, That ye love one another" (Jn 15:12). Paul says of it, "love is the fulfilling of the law" (Rom 13:10). And also, "Bear ye one another's burdens" (Gal 6:2). For by what can the law of Christ be understood more than by love, which we truly fulfill when we bear our brethren's burdens on the basis of love?

11.5.17.en: This same law is called "double," because love, full of surpassing and zealous care, extends to all works of virtue. It is laid down in only two commandments, yet it reaches to a number beyond counting. For the beginning of the law is the love of God and the love of our neighbor (Mt 22:39-40)...

11.5.18.en: But "the love of God" is divided into three parts. For we are commanded to love our Creator [with all our heart, all our soul and all our might]. In this we must note that the holy Word commands us to be bound to the love of God. It does not tell us only how, but teaches us how far, by adding "all." For whoever desires to please God perfectly must leave nothing in himself for himself.

11.5.19.en: And the love of our neighbor comes in two commandments. On the one hand it was said by a righteous man: [Do this, that thou have no man whom thou hatest] (Tob 4:16). On the other hand the Truth says, "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them" (Mt 7:12). By these two commandments evil conduct is restrained and good conduct is laid upon us.

11.5.20.en: * Therefore the law of God is rightly called "double," for while it has love as its principle, as soon as it takes possession of the mind it kindles it in double ways with countless works... Paul declares the doubleness of this very law in a fitting way, enumerating the following: "Love suffereth long, and is kind; love envieth not; love vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil; rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth" (1 Cor 13:4-6).

11.5.22.en: Second: the double understanding means a continual increase without interruption. As long as we are in the body we shall not cease to seek growth in wisdom, knowledge and love. Indeed, some of the Fathers see that this growth does not stop even in eternal life. For the more the believer gazes upon God and receives a deeper union, the more he grows without ceasing in wisdom, knowledge and love. He will never cease to sing continually: [Behold, all things have become new] (Rev 21:5).

11.5.23.en: * Although everyone constantly seeks more knowledge, it remains incomplete in all things in relation to its true perfection, until the time comes when that which is perfect is come and that which is in part is done away.

11.5.24.en: St. Basil the Great * He encourages her and urges her not to sit idle there, but to come out to Him, and to try to see Him neither through the windows nor in a mirror, darkly, but to go to Him and see Him face to face (Song 2:9). For now, since she cannot see Him, He stands thus behind her and not before her; He stands behind her back, behind the wall (Song 2:9).

11.5.25.en: Origen: Zophar did not know his limits. If what he urges on Job is to seek a double knowledge, this is a holy request and good counsel; but by not keeping within bounds he declared in folly that what had befallen Job was less than he deserved, as though it were fitting for Job to expect more blows.

11.5.26.en: Here Pope Gregory (the Great) likens Zophar to a friend who accompanies his friend and goes with him into the forest to help him cut wood, and then, in his lack of wisdom, he swings the axe, the head of the axe flies off, and it smashes the head of his companion. Instead of helping him to cut the wood, in folly he cut off his head!

11.5.27.en: It is fitting for us, in wisdom, to understand the limits of rebuke and reproof, and the limits of discipline, so that we do not crush our brethren. As the Apostle Paul says concerning the discipline of the young man who wanted to cling to his father's wife and whom he ordered to be cut off, he returned to say, "So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him" (2 Cor 2:7-8). For he had received enough, and the discipline had reached its goal, and the matter had become extremely serious; for if the penitent does not find the tender embrace of the Church, despair enslaves him and his soul perishes. As they were bound to discipline him by cutting him off, now they are bound to confirm love toward him and renew it, so that his soul may rejoice in salvation.

11.5.28.en: * "Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth" [6]... Here we should know that Zophar rebuked the righteous man with great iniquity, in that he accused him wrongly... But the word of insult that was offered can be removed if we consider the root from which it sprang. Therefore the Lord rightly commanded through Moses: "As when a man goeth into the wood with his neighbour to hew wood, and his hand fetcheth a stroke with the axe to cut down the tree, and the head slippeth from the helve, and lighteth upon his neighbour, that he die; he shall flee unto one of those cities, and live: Lest the avenger of the blood pursue the slayer, while his heart is hot, and overtake him, because the way is long, and slay him" (Deut 19:5-6). For we go with a friend into the wood when we go with a neighbor to see our iniquities, and we hew wood when we cut off the evil deeds from the wicked with a godly aim; but the axe flies from our hand when the correction is very hard, and it strikes his neighbor and he dies, so that he who gave the rebuke has killed his hearer with the spirit of love. For the mind of the person rebuked is at once driven to hatred if he is condemned without regard for limits.

11.5.30.en: * Rebuke must be preceded by mercy, not by anger.

11.5.31.en: St. Augustine * It is not fitting for physicians to be angry with the sick, but they ought to oppose the diseases in order to heal the sick.

11.5.32.en: St. Basil the Great * Tend the flock not with weariness nor with scorn, as though you had authority over them, but as a good shepherd who gathers the lambs into his bosom, and strengthens those that are with young.

11.6.s.en: 3. God's perfection cannot be searched out

11.6.0.en: 7 "Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? 8 It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know? 9 The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.

11.6.1.en: "Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?" [7]

11.6.2.en: Zophar portrays the greatness and glory of God just as he portrays the folly and ignorance of man; therefore it is necessary to submit to Him and seek His mercy and care. No man can discover His wisdom, so how can he fault it?

11.6.3.en: Who can reach the depths of God, and who knows His end? However much you long for Him, however much you cling to Him and come to know His person, your knowledge of Him remains utterly incomplete. Do not imagine that you succeed in searching out His essence and perceiving the perfection of His truth. We perceive the reality of His existence, but we do not reach an understanding of His mysteries. It is like the eye that sees the ocean, but does not reach its end.

11.6.4.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem translated the word corresponding to "end" as "least": "Canst thou find out the traces of God, or come to the least of what the Almighty has made?" and he comments on this: [If the least of God's works is beyond comprehension, can the Creator of all these be comprehended?!]

11.6.5.en: * [Canst thou find a trace of the Lord? or canst thou reach the end of what the Almighty doeth?] That is, if, as you said before, you cannot find the trace of a ship (on the sea), nor of the flight of an eagle (in the air), who can find a trace of God's dispensations, or who can understand the hints of His divine providence which He accomplishes in succession?

11.6.6.en: * It is good to say this about God, but Zophar did not say it with a pure intention; rather, while glorifying God, he pronounces evil against the righteous man.

11.6.7.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * No one has yet discovered, or will discover, what God is in His nature and essence. The discovery takes place in the future. Let those who have thoughts about this search and think about what will come to pass in the future.

11.6.8.en: My mind, which is in the likeness of God, tells me that when that godlike and divine (I mean the mind and the intellect) is mingled with what is akin to it, when the image returns to its Archetype for which it longs, this seems to me to be the meaning of that great saying, that in the age to come we shall know even as also we are known.

11.6.9.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * Although everyone constantly seeks more knowledge, it remains incomplete in all things in relation to its true perfection, until the time comes when that which is perfect is come and that which is in part is done away.

11.6.10.en: St. Basil the Great Who can comprehend the depth of God's mysteries and His plan, or understand His works, or who can follow the trace of His steps? Thus man continues to enjoy ceaseless knowledge, and the further he advances, the more he perceives his inability to comprehend the depths of the mystery of God.

11.6.11.en: Through the Gospel thought, the Fathers give us the way into the mystery of the knowledge of God, namely love. The more our hearts are kindled with the practical love of Him, the more our inner sight is washed to recognize new depths. And the more we enter new depths in the knowledge of God, the more the flame of our love for Him increases, so that we despise temporal things and cling to the eternal.

11.6.12.en: * "Canst thou find the footsteps of God?" What does he call "the footsteps of God" but the compassions of His visitation? By this he stimulates us to advance toward the heavenly things when we respond to the breezes of His Spirit...

11.6.13.en: When the spiritual love of the Lord kindles the heart, He gives knowledge of a path to follow, as a kind of footsteps of God, like one who walks and leaves the prints of his feet upon the heart...

11.6.14.en: The psalmist was well skilled in following the footsteps of our Creator when he said, [My soul followeth hard after thee] (Ps 63:8), and when he desired to obtain a heavenly vision, [My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?] (Ps 42:2).

11.6.15.en: Almighty God is found in a clear sense when we trample underfoot the corruption of our death. Then He is seen by those who are lifted up to heaven in the radiance of His divine nature. In the present time, however, the grace of the Spirit poured out in our hearts lifts the soul from fleshly aims and raises it by despising temporal things, and the mind no longer looks downward at all that is desired from below, but is kindled with longing for the heavenly things.

11.6.17.en: * The tongue has no power to utter their manner (the divine mysteries); only the pure mind beholds them, and in them it delights and rejoices at seeing them, marvels and exults in their existence, is amazed and delighted at their being revealed to it; and it is amazed and caught up by them into their interior.

11.6.18.en: And in God it is swallowed up and taken captive by beholding His beauty, and is united with His glory and amazed.

11.6.19.en: No one who has entered into this looks with desire upon what is seen here.

11.6.20.en: No one who delights in these (mysteries) also tastes the sweetness of anything that is on earth.

11.6.21.en: No one who beholds their beauty looks upon the beauty of anything in our world as good.

11.6.22.en: No one who is made rich by their presence fails to despise the silver coin as dung.

11.6.23.en: No one who has become familiar with their presence and drunk with meditating on them fails to loathe in his eyes the gatherings of men and their companionship.

11.6.24.en: No one in whose soul and bones the love of Christ has been set free is also able to bear the filth of loathsome lust.

11.6.25.en: No one who has become a companion of the angels and familiar with their mysteries fails to reject the company of the world and its snares.

11.6.26.en: No one whose mind has been taken captive by the beauty of the Lord of all is also able to be taken captive by anything in this world with its desires.

11.6.27.en: No one who has bound his mind to God and to care for Him is also loosed from it by anything and bound to the worry of it.

11.6.29.en: "It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do?"

11.7.0.en: "deeper than hell; what canst thou know?" [8]

11.8.0.en: "The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea" [9].

11.8.1.en: If we cannot measure the height of the heavens, nor the depths of the abyss, nor the length of the earth, nor the breadth of the seas, how can we measure the Creator of them all? The psalmist says, "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it" (Ps 139:6), "thy judgments are a great deep" (Ps 36:6).

11.8.2.en: We lift up our eyes on high toward heaven, and we see God lofty, higher than it. Then our souls long to be freed from the bondage of the love of the world, by the work of the Holy Spirit of God, who flies with us as on the wings of a dove.

11.8.3.en: We look into the depths of the abyss, and we see the Lord in His love breaking down its bars and carrying us off into the divine embrace.

11.8.4.en: We roam over the wide earth, and we find it very narrow before the breadth of God's heart toward us, in which He embraces all humanity from Adam to the end of the ages, with a love that has no limit.

11.8.5.en: We look at the oceans and we count them as nothing before the surpassing deep of God's love.

11.8.6.en: * [He is higher than heaven, what canst thou do? deeper than hell, what canst thou know? longer than the earth, and broader than the sea] [8-9]. This must be understood in a spiritual sense. If anything pertaining to Him is understood in a bodily way, it is an evil thing. Now He is higher than heaven, since He rises above all things by the impossibility of comprehending His spiritual nature. He is deeper than the abyss, for in His loftiness He helps us who are below. He is longer than the earth in that He surpasses the measure of creation by the infinite continuance of His eternity. He is broader than the sea, being the ruler of the waves of temporal affairs, holding them back and bringing them to pass by His power.

11.8.8.en: * All these particulars point to man alone, who becomes "heaven" when he desires to attach himself to the heavenly things.

11.8.9.en: And he himself becomes an abyss when he lies prostrate, bound to the things below, entangled in temptations.

11.8.10.en: And he becomes "earth" when he multiplies good works through the fruitfulness of a steadfast hope.

11.8.11.en: And he becomes a sea when he is troubled with anxiety in some circumstances and is confused by the breath of his weakness.

11.8.12.en: God is higher than heaven in that we submit to the power of His authority, even when we rise above ourselves.

11.8.13.en: He is deeper than the abyss in that He judges the human mind itself, looking upon it in the midst of temptations.

11.8.14.en: He is longer than the earth by the fruits of our life which He gives us in the end. Our very hope in the present time grasps nothing.

11.8.15.en: He is broader than the sea, since the human mind, tossed about here and there, throws up many passions concerning the things to come.

11.8.16.en: The psalmist set his heart on high, and yet he felt that he had not yet reached God, so he says: [Wonderful exceedingly is thy knowledge of me; it is mighty, I cannot attain unto it] (Ps 139:6). Paul knew that which is deeper than the abyss when he examined his heart, but he feared God's judgment, which searches more thoroughly. He said: [For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord] (see 1 Cor 4:4).

11.9.0.en: "If he cut off, and shut up, or gather together, then who can hinder him?" [10]

11.9.1.en: Zophar reached the very conclusion that Job had already reached concerning God's absolute wisdom: "Behold, he taketh away, who can hinder him? who will say unto him, What doest thou?" (Job 12:9) and "Thou knowest that I am not guilty; and there is none that can deliver out of thine hand" (Job 7:10).

11.9.2.en: If He "cut off" by death, or shut someone up in prison, or gathered him as in a net of snares, who can prevent Him? Who is able to stand before God's judgment or resist His work? Who has the authority to object to God's judgments?

11.9.3.en: * [If he overturn all things, who shall contradict him? or who can say unto him, Why doest thou this?] [10] The Lord "overturns" heaven when He destroys the height of man's contemplations by His terrible, hidden command. He lays waste the abyss when He allows a person's soul to be terrified under its trials and fall to the utmost extremes. And He casts down the earth when He removes the fruits of good works by pouring misfortunes upon them. And He overturns the sea when He refutes the wavering (waves) of our hesitating spirit by a sudden terror.

11.9.4.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem Marcion, in the second century AD, and also his followers, stumbled at the expressions in the Old Testament concerning divine wrath. I have already devoted a special section to the concept of "the wrath of God" in the book Brotherly Love, chapter 8, on wrath. God does not strike anyone down and does not shut anyone up; what the Holy Bible says about God's wrath is by way of presenting some divine matters in human language that we can understand.

11.9.5.en: God does not have human passions, for He is "love"!

11.9.6.en: * When we read of the wrath and anger of the Lord, we should not understand the word according to the meaning of an ignoble human emotion, but in a sense befitting God, who is free from every passion or blemish. Hence we should perceive from this that He is the Judge and the Avenger of all the unjust things that are committed in this world.

11.9.7.en: And by the logic of these terms and their meaning we should fear Him as the One to be feared who recompenses us for our deeds, and fear to do anything against His will. For human nature is accustomed to fear those whom it knows to be angry, and is afraid of offending them, as is the case with certain judges who have reached the height of justice.

11.9.8.en: The avenging wrath is usually feared by those who are tormented by the accusation of their consciences; certainly not because this tendency exists in the minds of those who will keep fairness in their judgments. But while they are in the throes of this fear, the judge's inclinations toward them are marked by justice, impartiality, and respect for the law which he carries out. And this, however gently and kindly he conducts himself, is stigmatized with the harshest epithets of anger and fierce wrath by those who have been punished rightly and justly.

11.10.0.en: 11 "For he knoweth vain men: he seeth wickedness also; will he not then consider it? 12 As for man, he is empty, void of understanding, and man is born like a wild ass's colt. 13 If thou prepare thine heart, and stretch out thine hands toward him; 14 If thou put away the iniquity that is in thine hand, and let not wickedness dwell in thy tabernacle, for he knoweth vain men: he seeth wickedness also; will he not then consider it? [11]

11.10.1.en: We know of Him the very least, but He perceives all our secrets, even those hidden from us. He knows men of wickedness even if we or they count themselves righteous, and He sees the iniquity we commit in secret. The wicked are exposed before Him, and evil cannot be hidden from Him. "Will he not then consider it?" That is, will He stand passive before the wicked and evil, even if He overlooks it for a time?

11.10.2.en: * [For he knoweth the vanity of men, and when he seeth iniquity, will he not then consider it?] [11]... Here the order is well observed, for he first describes vanity as being known, and after that iniquity as being considered. For every iniquity is vain, but not every vanity is iniquity. For we practice vain things as long as we do what is transitory. In this the thing passes away from the eyes of him who holds it, and it is said to be "vain." The psalmist says, "Surely every man walketh in a vain shew" (Ps 39:6).

11.11.0.en: "As for man, he is empty, void of understanding, and man is born like a wild ass's colt" [12].

11.11.1.en: Zophar says that man himself, after the fall, became empty and void of understanding, because he deprived himself of God's wisdom. He became "like the beasts that perish" (Ps 49:20). He became foolish like the wild ass (the wild ass's colt) that is accustomed to dwell in the wilderness. In his folly he thinks himself wise, and so he does not want to submit to God's judgments, but resists, thinking that he knows truth and justice.

11.11.2.en: What Zophar said is a truth into which man has fallen in general, but what mars his words is that he means Job and not his friends, counting him in the rank of the foolish and useless wild beasts. Yet when he speaks of himself, he counts himself wise, offering sincere and effective counsel!

11.11.3.en: * [Mortal, born of woman, like the wild ass's colt] [12]. By these words he points to Job, making him equal to the wild ass's colt. For he said: [For the arrows of the Lord are in my flesh... Doth the wild ass bray without cause, unless he is seeking food?] (Job 6:4-5). Craftily Zophar says: why does he speak of a mortal born of a woman, that is, of a man born of a man, since Job himself compares himself to the wild ass's colt? Therefore Zophar says: [In vain he hides in his reasonings] [12]. By these vain, useless words he brings Job down to triviality, for Zophar says that he must howl very much and not sigh much, avoiding being a man. He compares him to a colt that is starving.

11.11.4.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * [The empty (vain) man swells up in pride] this is the end of vanity. Pride corrupts the heart with sin and makes it insolent in iniquity, so that, by ignoring its iniquity, the soul does not grieve over the loss of its innocence, and it is struck with blindness as a just recompense, and perhaps is also separated from humility. The heart often takes back for itself evil desires, casting off the yoke of the fear of the Lord, as though it were becoming free to commit evil. It struggles to bring evil into action, indulging itself.

11.11.6.en: If man has descended to the folly of some animals, even of insects, through the pride of his heart and his exalting himself against God, the source of wisdom, then the Wisdom of God became man, in order to lift him up to heavenly wisdom, to enjoy Him and be united with Him. By the divine Incarnation, especially by the Ascension of the Lord Christ, we were lifted up in Him from the degradation of the animals to heavenly wisdom.

11.11.7.en: * Look at our nature, how it was brought low and then raised up. For it was not possible to descend further than man descended, nor possible to ascend higher than Christ ascended... Paul makes this clear when he says: "He that descended is the same also that ascended." And where did He descend? "Into the lower parts of the earth," and He ascended "far above all heavens" (Eph 4:9-10).

11.11.8.en: Understand from this who it is that ascended...!

11.11.9.en: I meditate on the unworthiness of our race until I perceive the honor we have received through the merciful compassions of the Lord, full of tenderness. For we were nothing but dust and ashes...

11.11.10.en: We have become more foolish than the irrational animals, for man is compared to the irrational animals, and has become like them (Ps 49:20). And when man becomes thus like them, he is worse than they. For they are so by the decree of their nature, but our lack of understanding, we who are a creation adorned with reason, is by our own will...

11.11.11.en: And so, when you hear of man that he has become like the irrational animals, do not think that he has become equal to them, but lower than they. Not in the sense that he descended to a level below them, but that we, being human beings, have come to this extreme degree of dullness...

11.11.12.en: This is what Isaiah teaches plainly, saying: "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider" (Isa 1:3).

11.11.13.en: But let us not be troubled because of our former transgressions, for where sin abounded, grace did much more abound (Rom 5:20).

11.11.14.en: You have seen how we have become more foolish than the animals; do you wish to see how we have become more unreasoning than the birds?!

11.11.15.en: "The turtledove and the swallow that chirps observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the LORD" (Jer 8:7).

11.11.16.en: See how we have become more foolish than the ass and the ox and the birds of the heaven, the turtledove and the swallow; do you also wish to see to what our folly has reached?!

11.11.17.en: He sends us to the ant to learn wisdom from it: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise" (Prov 6:6).

11.11.18.en: We have become pupils of the ant, we who were created in the image and likeness of God. But our Creator was not the cause; we ourselves are the cause, since we did not wish to remain in His image and likeness.

11.11.19.en: And why do I speak of the ant only, when we have become more dull than stones? Shall I offer proof of this? "Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD'S controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth: for the LORD hath a controversy with his people" (Mic 6:2).

11.11.20.en: He judges man, summoning the foundations of the earth... because men have become duller than the foundations of the earth.

11.11.21.en: To what extent of folly do they still wish to go?! For they have become more foolish than the ass, more insensible than the ox, more without understanding than the turtledove and the swallow, more without wisdom than the ant (a), duller than stones, and they even resemble the vipers (see Ps 58:4-5)...

11.11.22.en: And why do I speak any more of the irrational creation, when we have come to be called (in our evil) children of the devil, as He says, "Ye are of your father the devil" (Jn 8:44).

11.11.23.en: And yet, although we are dull of senses, ungrateful, foolish and harder than stones, and such has become our degradation and unworthiness... today our nature has been lifted above all creation!

11.12.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "If thou prepare thine heart, and stretch out thine hands toward him" [13].

11.12.1.en: If God's dimensions cannot be comprehended, so to speak, and He is the One who holds authority and knows all things, then on the other hand man cannot comprehend the perfection of God and the perfection of His knowledge, nor even the mysteries of human nature itself. Therefore it was fitting for man, instead of criticizing God's actions, to turn to Him in prayer and remove everything foreign to God, of iniquity and wickedness, and then God lifts up His face and grants him countless blessings.
